title: Challenge #113: Query-Efficient Sim-to-Real Quantum-Gate Calibration
lede: The local control landscape has d²−1 curved directions, but model mismatch rotates their pulse-space orientation; model-informed search is therefore efficient when the basis is valid, while device-triggered relinearization is needed to retain the advantage at larger drift mismatch.

sections.title: Challenge
sections.note: What issue #113 asks, and the precise claim tested here.

blocks.text: A differentiable device model can produce a high-fidelity gate and exact pulse derivatives cheaply, but the physical device differs from that model and exposes only expensive, noisy measurements. Issue #113 asks whether the model Hessian identifies a low-dimensional pulse subspace that reduces closed-loop calibration cost, where that transfer fails as the model-device gap grows, and whether modest adaptation can recover the saving.

Near a model optimum, write $U_{\mathrm{target}}^\dagger U(\theta)=e^{iA}$. Gate fidelity is insensitive to the identity part of the Hermitian generator $A$, so only the traceless generators contribute curvature. Their dimension is $d^2-1$: three for one qubit and fifteen for two qubits. This fixes the maximum local curvature rank, but it does **not** guarantee that a basis computed from an imperfect model keeps the correct orientation in pulse-parameter space.

Closed-loop evaluations consume real experiments and measurement shots, and derivative-free optimization becomes expensive as the number of pulse controls grows. A reliable reduced coordinate system can move most computation into the simulator while preserving the device's ability to correct model error.

pairs: Quantum Harness issue #113 — Sim-to-Real for Quantum Gates
Single-qubit X gate (d=2, P=20) and two-qubit CNOT (d=4, P=40)
Two completed figures; 15 held-out finite-shot runs per condition
Simulated drift-Hamiltonian mismatch; no real-hardware claim

sections.title: Approach
sections.note: A strict model/device split and an honest count of every black-box query.

blocks.text: The model dynamics are $H(t;\theta)=H_0+\sum_a u_a(t;\theta)H_a$. We first optimize $\theta^*$ with model gradients, compute the Hessian or endpoint Jacobian at that pulse, and form an orthonormal basis $V_k$. Closed-loop candidates are restricted to $\theta=\theta^*+V_kc$. The simulated device uses $H_{0,\mathrm{true}}=H_0+\varepsilon\Delta H$, with $\|\Delta H\|_F=\|H_0\|_F$, and returns only a binomial finite-shot estimate of scalar fidelity. The loop never sees the held-out Hamiltonian, its Jacobian, $\varepsilon$, a gradient, or exact fidelity.

pairs: Leading eigenvectors of the Hessian at the nominal model optimum
One precomputed basis from stacked, block-normalized endpoint Jacobians of the nominal model plus 15 declared perturbation models
Start with nominal k=15; after a failed device-only certificate, recompute a k=20 ensemble-Jacobian basis at the device-selected pulse and continue
Five unseen drift seeds × three independent shot-noise seeds per ε; training and test seeds are disjoint
65,536 shots per query; every query and shot counted

blocks.text: **Five-point coordinate scan.** For each reduced coordinate, the device is queried at offsets $\{-h,-h/2,0,h/2,h\}$ with $h=0.3$. A one-dimensional quadratic is fitted; if its minimum lies inside the interval and is convex, that vertex is also queried, and the best measured point is retained. This transparent, fixed-cost pass is used for the single-qubit study and as the initial nominal k=15 stage of the adaptive two-qubit loop.

**COBYQA.** For the two-qubit fixed-space comparison and adaptive recovery stages, COBYQA constructs and updates a local quadratic model of the scalar loss inside a trust region, without device gradients. It is used after the coordinate scan because coupled motion among 20–30 reduced coordinates is better represented by a multivariate trust-region model than by another independent-axis pass.

A single favorable noisy observation is not accepted. The selected pulse is queried seven more times and succeeds only if the Wilson upper bound on infidelity, implemented with $z=1.96$, is at most $10^{-3}$. This is conservative relative to a nominal one-sided 95% bound. Failed runs are right-censored at budget+1: 501 queries in Figure 1 and 701 in Figure 2. Curves report the median and interquartile range across 15 runs; percentages are certified success rates.

sections.title: Results
sections.note: Two figures answer the intrinsic-dimension, query-saving, and mismatch-failure questions.

blocks.text: Figure 1 — The d²−1 geometry is real and useful

items.caption: Passed. (a) The differentiable model supplies a warm-start pulse and reduced basis; only finite-shot scalar loss crosses the device boundary. (b) Normalized Hessian spectra at model optima have numerical rank 3 for the single-qubit X gate and 15 for the two-qubit CNOT, using a relative 10⁻⁶ threshold, exactly matching d²−1. (c) At ε=0.3, single-qubit nominal spaces with k<3 never certify, while the informed k=3 space certifies 15/15 runs in a median 25 queries. A random k=3 space certifies 0/15; the raw 20-dimensional space certifies 15/15 but requires a median 126 queries. Error bars are interquartile ranges; 501 denotes right-censored failures.

blocks.label: Issue claim confirmed in the valid-transfer regime
blocks.why: The curvature rank tracks d²−1 across d=2 and d=4, and the correctly oriented model subspace cuts the single-qubit median query count by about 5× relative to the raw search.

blocks.text: Figure 2 — Fixed directions fail under mismatch; triggered relinearization recovers

items.caption: Passed within the declared drift benchmark. (a) For the CNOT, fixed nominal Hessian spaces show the dimension-cost trade-off: at ε=0.1, k=15 already gives 15/15 success with median 238 queries, whereas k=20 and 30 cost 313 and 461. At ε=0.5, the same fixed k=15 space falls to 3/15 success; k=20 reaches 9/15 and k=30 reaches 14/15, but at median censored costs 414 and 599. (b) Fixed nominal k=15 is cheapest only when transfer is good; fixed ensemble k=30 is robust but expensive. The device-triggered k=15→20 protocol certifies all 45 held-out runs, with median queries 97, 330, and 330 at ε=0.1, 0.3, and 0.5. Percentages label certified success; error bars are interquartile ranges; 701 denotes right-censored failures.

blocks.label: Failure mode identified and recovered
blocks.why: A fixed top-d²−1 basis is not uniformly robust because mismatch rotates its pulse-space orientation. Blindly carrying more fixed directions improves reachability but spends more queries; a certificate-triggered basis update attains 100% success here with at most 20 active directions.

sections.title: Highlight
sections.note: What is established, what is new, and what is not claimed.

blocks.text: Yes: the model Hessian exposes the predicted $d^2-1$ local geometry and, when its orientation transfers, it reduces black-box calibration cost substantially. The sweet spot is not a universal fixed $k=d^2-1$ under arbitrary mismatch. The observed failure is a rotation of useful pulse directions, so the practical solution is to test transfer with device data and update the basis only when needed.

The key distinction is between **intrinsic physical dimension** and **model-dependent pulse-space orientation**. The method retains a strict black-box boundary and uses a statistically defined device certificate to decide when the inexpensive nominal search is sufficient and when model-side relinearization is warranted.

The result turns the issue's qualitative warning about the sim-to-real gap into a measured design rule. Use the smallest physically motivated basis first; do not enlarge it merely because mismatch exists; trigger a new local basis when the observed device certificate says the current coordinates are inadequate.

This pattern can reduce experimental calibration effort whenever a differentiable surrogate is available but imperfect. The evidence here is deliberately limited to simulated drift-Hamiltonian mismatch, two gate sizes, and the declared finite-shot protocol. It does not establish performance on real hardware or under every form of device error.
